interviewQuestions.question: Why are random reads so much slower than sequential reads on a hard disk?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd anchor the answer in the two mechanical costs every HDD access pays: **seek time** (moving the arm to the right track) and **rotational latency** (waiting for the platter to spin the right sector under the head). Together these commonly cost several milliseconds — an eternity compared to the actual data transfer.

Sequential access lays data out so consecutive reads stay on the same or adjacent tracks, paying that mechanical cost roughly once and then streaming at the drive's full transfer rate. Random access, by contrast, means each request likely lands on a different track, so the drive pays seek time and rotational latency again and again — one request at a time.

Concretely, that's the difference between a drive sustaining ~150-200 MB/s sequentially but only a few hundred IOPS randomly — almost all the time in a random workload goes to moving metal, not moving bits.

**Testing:** whether you understand that the *mechanism* (not just the fact) behind sequential-vs-random performance is mechanical motion, since that's the reasoning that also explains why SSDs closed this gap.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why random access is slow on HDDs

interviewQuestions.question: If HDDs are so much slower for random access, why do they still get used in production systems today?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd point to cost per gigabyte as the deciding factor — HDDs remain substantially cheaper per unit of capacity than SSDs, which matters enormously at large scale. For workloads that are cold (rarely accessed), large, and accessed mostly sequentially — backups, archival logs, cold object storage tiers — the latency penalty barely matters because you're not doing scattered random lookups against that data anyway.

I'd give a concrete example: a company storing years of compliance logs that are almost never read, but must be retained, will happily accept HDD-class latency in exchange for a fraction of the storage cost, especially multiplied across petabytes.

The boundary is clear though — anything latency-sensitive, or accessed with a random pattern (a database's primary storage, for instance), moves to SSD/NVMe, because the mechanical latency wall genuinely can't be engineered away on a spinning disk.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about a storage decision as a cost/latency/access-pattern trade-off, rather than assuming 'faster is always better.'
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why HDDs persist despite being slower

interviewQuestions.question: What's the difference between short-stroking a hard disk and just buying a smaller-capacity model, and why would anyone deliberately waste capacity like that?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd explain short-stroking as a technique that trades away unused capacity specifically to buy back mechanical performance, which is a different lever than simply buying a smaller drive.

A disk's outer tracks are physically longer than its inner tracks, so at a fixed rotational speed, the outer tracks pass under the head faster — meaning higher sequential transfer rates on the outer edge of the platter than near the spindle. Short-stroking deliberately restricts all reads and writes to a narrow band of outer tracks (partitioning away the rest), which does two things: it shrinks the **seek distance** the arm ever has to travel, since every track in use is physically close together, and it keeps every access on the platter's fastest-spinning region. Buying a genuinely smaller-capacity drive doesn't give you either benefit — a smaller drive's platters are still (typically) the same physical size and speed, so its inner-vs-outer transfer-rate spread and full-stroke seek distance are unchanged; only short-stroking specifically restricts *where on the existing platter* data lives.

Concrete use case: before SSDs became affordable for performance-sensitive tiers, database and video-editing shops would short-stroke enterprise HDDs — accepting maybe 50% capacity loss — specifically to cut worst-case seek time and boost sustained throughput for latency-sensitive workloads, when an SSD wasn't yet an economical option.

**Testing:** understanding that short-stroking manipulates *where* on the mechanism data lives, distinct from simply buying less capacity.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Short-stroking as a mechanical performance trade-off
